title: Steel Front Bumper Selection for the LJ

parts.name: Smittybilt XRC Front Bumper with D-ring mounts

summary: The LJ's front bumper mount is identical to every TJ and uses the same 2-bolt frame-horn attachment shared by all 1997–2006 Wranglers — so the aftermarket is enormous. The difference on an LJ is intent: this rig is heavier and often used for multi-day overland trips, which means a winch-capable bumper isn't optional, it's the default. Plan around a 12,000-lb winch from the start.
description:
The factory plastic front bumper on the LJ is a liability the moment you leave pavement. It offers no recovery points, no winch platform, and cracks on the first moderate brush contact. A steel bumper is one of the highest-value first upgrades on any Wrangler, and on the LJ — which regularly carries camping gear and travels farther from the trailhead — it's especially important.

The Smittybilt XRC is the benchmark budget steel bumper. It's heavy-gauge steel, includes integrated D-ring mounts rated to 4.75 tons, and has a center winch plate that accepts all standard winch footprints. The Rough Country stubby is even cheaper but sacrifices the wing plates that protect the headlight corners. Both fit without modification using the factory frame horns. If you're on a strict budget and want a winch mounted this weekend, the XRC is the call.

The Poison Spyder BFH (Big Ugly Heavy) is a step up in fitment quality, approach angle, and plate thickness. It's purpose-built for wheeling — the design specifically prioritizes protecting the grille and lights while maximizing approach angle. Rugged Ridge's HD bumper is a solid compromise: better steel gauge than Smittybilt, integrated light tabs, and a quality winch plate for less than Poison Spyder. Both include D-ring mounts and proper bolt-in installation.

GenRight makes an aluminum front bumper that saves roughly 30 lbs compared to an equivalent steel bumper — meaningful on a platform that already carries more weight than a TJ. The aluminum construction doesn't sacrifice strength for the application; it's designed for hard trail use. Metalclad builds fully custom steel bumpers at the high end. At this tier you're paying for precision fit, lighter weight, and the option to specify winch position and accessory tabs.

Any bumper you choose for an LJ should include a proper winch plate rated for at least 12,000 lbs. The LJ is a heavier vehicle than the TJ — roughly 200 lbs more — and when loaded for overland it can exceed 4,000 lbs. A 9,500-lb winch that's adequate on a stripped TJ is undersized for an LJ with a roof rack and gear aboard. Build winch capacity in from day one, not as a bolt-on afterthought with an incompatible bumper.

title: Rear Bumper with Swing-Out Tire Carrier for the LJ

parts.name: Smittybilt SRC Rear Bumper with Tire Carrier

summary: The LJ's 103.5-inch wheelbase is a genuine advantage at the rear: a swing-out spare tire carrier hangs farther from the back of the cab, which improves departure angle and keeps the spare from dragging on obstacles. The rear bumper is also your primary rear recovery attachment point — a factory receiver hitch is not a rated recovery anchor.
description:
The factory LJ rear bumper is plastic with a tow receiver — adequate for a ball hitch and nothing else. Swapping to a steel bumper with integrated D-ring mounts and a proper swing-out tire carrier is the right move for any LJ used on trail or overland. It adds rear recovery capability, protects the rear crossmember, and handles a full-size spare without bending.

The swing-out tire carrier must be rated for the spare you're running. A 35-inch tire on a steel wheel weighs 65–80 lbs. Cheap carriers with undersized pins and weld quality will crack and sag within a season of trail use. Verify the carrier's stated tire size rating before buying. All three bumpers listed here are rated for at least a 35-inch spare; budget-tier carriers from generic brands often are not.

The Smittybilt SRC rear bumper bolt-in fits all TJ and LJ Wranglers. It includes D-ring mounts, a swing-out carrier rated for 35-inch tires, and a receiver hitch. Build quality is acceptable for the price. The swing-out arm uses a two-pin design and gets loose over time; plan to apply thread locker to the hinge bolts after the first season.

Rock Hard 4x4 makes a YJ/TJ/LJ-specific rear bumper that is a noticeable step up in steel gauge and weld quality. The swing-out arm is tighter, the D-ring mounts are fully welded, and it bolts to the factory frame mounting locations without modification. For an LJ used regularly on trail, Rock Hard is the value choice.

The Poison Spyder Bombshell is a heavy, high-quality steel bumper with a robust swing-out and full D-ring integration. It's heavier than the Rock Hard but built to take direct hits. At the premium tier you're also getting better paint prep and rust resistance. For a dedicated rock crawler or a high-mileage overlander, it's worth it.

The integrated D-ring mounts on these bumpers are rated recovery points. The factory tow receiver is NOT — never run a recovery strap through a ball hitch or a factory bumper loop. With a proper steel bumper installed, you have four rated recovery points (two front, two rear) to work from.

title: Rock Sliders and Rocker Guards for the LJ
summary: The LJ's longer wheelbase means its rocker panels are exposed over a longer span than a TJ's, and the unibody-adjacent floor rails that run along the bottom of the tub take the hit when you highside a rock or stuff a wheel into a ledge. Frame-mounted rock sliders are the answer — not the decorative step sliders you find at a truck accessories shop.
description:
The distinction between a rock slider and a step slider matters: a step slider has a step tread welded to thin-wall tube and mounts to the body, not the frame. It will crumple into the body on a side hit. A proper rock slider is 2-inch or larger DOM tube, frame-mounted with welded brackets that transfer the load to the frame rails, and designed to slide over a rock rather than catch and fold.

Every rock slider on this list mounts to the LJ's frame — specifically the rocker pinch weld support brackets and the frame outriggers. Body-mounted sliders are not adequate for trail use. On the LJ, the body floor and tub are vulnerable to side loading and the unibody design means body damage is expensive to repair. Get sliders that mount to the frame and take the hit there.

Warn's sliders are a proven fit for TJ/LJ Wranglers. They're 2-inch DOM tube, frame-mounted, and have a high enough clearance profile to avoid dragging on most terrain. The install is bolt-in for TJ-spec frames, and the LJ uses the same frame locations. These are among the cleaner-looking options without the step tread. Price is fair for the quality.

GenRight's aluminum sliders save weight compared to steel — roughly 15 lbs per side — while maintaining structural strength for trail sliding. The aluminum construction won't rust, which matters if the LJ lives in a wet climate or sees salt. GenRight specifies LJ fitment; confirm when ordering that the length matches the longer LJ rocker. At $700 they're the premium pick but justified for an overland rig that will carry weight.

If you are looking at sliders with a step tread, rubberized inserts, or any description suggesting they function as a step to enter the vehicle, skip them. They are not trail protection. The only time a step is acceptable is if the slider is frame-mounted heavy-gauge tube that also happens to have a step — not a step bracket with thin steel tube as an afterthought.

title: Skid Plate Kit for the LJ

parts.name: Skid Row Offroad LJ Full Skid Kit
Rock Hard 4x4 Patriot Skid Plate System

citations.title: Skid Row Offroad LJ skid kits

summary: Skid plates are the unglamorous armor that saves the drivetrain: the LJ's oil pan, transfer case, and gas tank all hang within striking distance of terrain, and the gas tank location behind the rear axle sits lower on the LJ than on a 2-door TJ due to the longer wheelbase geometry. The order of priority is oil pan first, transfer case second, gas tank third — then anything else.
description:
The LJ's longer body positions the gas tank farther rearward and lower relative to the axle than on a TJ. This is an important difference: TJ skid kits often do not extend to cover the LJ's gas tank correctly, and some won't mount at all. Confirm LJ-specific fitment before ordering.

The oil pan is the most exposed component under an LJ. A single rock strike on a hard trail can crack it and strand you. The factory has no oil pan skid. A 1/4-inch steel skid plate bolted to the engine mount crossmember is the fix. Every full kit includes this; if you're doing it piecemeal, start here.

The NP231 (non-Rubicon) and NP241OR (Rubicon) transfer cases hang below the floor behind the transmission. A transfer case hit is expensive and immediate. The skid here wraps the transfer case in steel and ties into the frame. Most mid-tier and premium kits include a 3/16-inch or thicker plate here.

The LJ's gas tank position behind the rear axle makes it more vulnerable than on a standard TJ. A punctured tank is a fire and an abandonment. The Skid Row Offroad LJ kit specifically addresses this geometry with a rear skid that extends far enough to protect the tank. This is the skid most likely to be missed or undersized on a TJ-fit kit — verify coverage before buying.

Skid Row Offroad makes the most comprehensive LJ-specific kit and is the recommended choice for a full build. Rock Hard is solid steel, slightly thicker material, and bolts up cleanly. Rugged Ridge's entry-level kit is adequate for mild trail use but uses thinner material and doesn't cover the gas tank on the LJ. If budget forces a choice, get Rugged Ridge for the oil pan and TC now and plan the tank skid next.

title: The Dana 44 Rear: Why the LJ Starts Ahead

citations.title: LJ Wrangler specs — CJ Pony Parts

summary: The single biggest reason the LJ is worth more than a same-year TJ on the trail: it left the factory with a Dana 44 rear axle standard. Where the regular TJ shipped a c-clip Dana 35 that owners rush to replace, the LJ owner starts with the axle everyone else is upgrading to.
description:
The LJ Unlimited came with a Dana 44 rear on every trim, and the 2005–2006 Rubicon added a Dana 44 up front as well. That matters because the Dana 35 is the classic Wrangler weak link — c-clip shafts that snap under a locked rear on 33s, and tubes that bend. The LJ's Dana 44 has larger shafts, a bigger ring gear, and no c-clip failure mode, so it shrugs off 33s and takes 35s with a locker and the right shafts.

Confirm it with a glance: the Dana 44 cover is the familiar hexagonal shape, and the build sheet/axle tag gives the ratio. Non-Rubicon LJs run 3.73 gears; the Rubicon runs 4.10 front and rear with factory air lockers. The front on non-Rubicon LJs is still a Dana 30, so the front is the limiting member on a hard build, not the rear.

For 33s and a daily-driven LJ, leave the Dana 44 rear alone and put your money into the front Dana 30, steering, and lift. For 35s and a locker, add chromoly shafts and a quality locker — the housing is up to it. When you regear for bigger tires, gear the front Dana 30 to match exactly; a mismatched front and rear ratio will bind the transfer case and destroy tires.

The LJ's standard Dana 44 rear is a head start the TJ owner has to buy. Build the front and the steering to its level, and you have a balanced rig.

title: Fender Flare Upgrade for Wider Tires on the LJ
summary: The LJ's factory fender flares are the same style as TJ flares — a molded plastic lip with about 3.5 inches of coverage past the fender lip. They clear stock 30-inch tires with room to spare and 31s without rubbing at stock height. Go to 33s and you'll be cutting or replacing them. Go to 35s and you'll need a lift, flare replacement, and possibly front fender trimming regardless of flare style.
description:
This is a job most owners do themselves because the factory flares are plastic, bolt-on, and replaceable without any drama. The technique depends on how much lift you're running and how wide your tires are. On a 3.5-inch lift with 33x12.5s, flat replacement flares are the cleanest solution. On a 2-inch lift with 33x10.5s, careful trimming of the factory flares often works.

Flat flares replace the factory molded flares with a flat, wider piece of steel or aluminum. They extend the fender coverage outward without the raised lip shape, which means more clearance for wider tires. The Smittybilt SRC flat fenders are steel and work; they're a bit heavy and the finish is basic. The Rugged Ridge Arcus flares are a nicer looking option with a textured finish that holds up better. Both bolt to the existing TJ/LJ fender mounting holes without drilling. This is the cleanest upgrade for a 33-tire build.

If you'd rather not spend money on flares yet, trimming the factory units is an option. Score the inside edge with a grinder or die grinder, flex the flare until it snaps clean, and deburr the edge. A heat gun helps the plastic trim without cracking. This costs almost nothing and works for 33s on a 3-inch lift without rubbing. The result doesn't look factory-clean but it functions correctly and keeps the budget elsewhere.

At 2 inches of lift on 33x10.5R15 tires, trimming the factory flares or doing nothing often works without rubbing. At 3–4 inches on 33x12.5R15, flat replacement flares are recommended. At 4.5 inches or more on 35s, plan to trim the inner fender liner in addition to replacing the flares — the tire's radius at full articulation will contact the inner liner at the top of the stroke without it.

title: Mild Trail Build: 3.5" Lift, 33s, Bumper, Skids, Recovery — LJ
skills_required: planning a build in the right order

parts.name: Coil lift kit 3.5" (LJ-compatible, e.g. Rubicon Express Super-Flex)
Steel front bumper with winch plate (e.g. Smittybilt XRC)
Skid plate kit (oil pan + TC, LJ-specific)
Recovery kit: strap + shackles + traction boards

citations.title: Rubicon Express LJ Super-Flex lift kit
LJ Wrangler tire and lift guide — Quadratec

summary: The LJ's mild trail build does not need lockers, regears, or axle swaps to be genuinely useful on most trails. The 4.0L with 33s on a 3.5-inch lift and the right geometry corrections is a capable, well-mannered rig that handles 80% of trails without drama. Total cost runs $2,500-$5,000 depending on how much you do yourself and which tier of parts you choose.
description:
This recipe keeps the Dana 30 front and Dana 44 rear intact. It is the build that proves the LJ does not need to be expensive to be capable. Spend the money on the lift, tires, protection, and recovery, and save the axle work for when you outgrow this.

A 3.5-inch coil kit is the foundation. The Rubicon Express Super-Flex is the LJ-specific recommendation: it includes progressive-rate coils sized for the LJ's wheelbase, extended brake lines, and sway-bar disconnects. At this lift height, an adjustable front track bar is mandatory to re-center the front axle and prevent death wobble onset. Install both together. Ordering the lift without the track bar is half the job.

33x12.5R15 on 15x8-inch steel wheels with 3.75-inch backspacing. This combination fits a 3.5-inch lift without additional fender trimming on most LJs, though trimming the inner liner is often needed at full articulation. A set of five BFGoodrich K02 or Cooper Discoverer AT3 tires plus Pro Comp or Mickey Thompson steelies runs about $1,000. Get five wheels; a matching spare is important when running oversized rubber far from a tire shop.

Install a steel front bumper with an integrated winch plate before you need it. Even without a winch mounted yet, the bumper gives you rated D-ring recovery points and protects the grille. The Smittybilt XRC is the budget-correct choice at this build tier. When budget allows, add the 12,000-lb winch to this plate.

Oil pan and transfer case skids are the minimum; add the LJ-specific gas tank skid as soon as budget allows. The Skid Row Offroad LJ kit does all three. At 3.5 inches of lift, the belly is more exposed than stock and protection is not optional.

A rated 30-foot snatch strap, two 3/4-inch D-ring shackles, and a pair of traction boards covers the vast majority of trail self-recovery situations. The strap-and-boards kit handles most soft-surface recoveries; add the winch when budget allows.

The LJ on 33s with a 3.5-inch lift and the 4.0L's factory 3.73 gears drives comfortably and handles moderate wheeling including rock gardens, forest roads, and sand. The longer wheelbase means better road stability than a similarly-built TJ and less tip concern on off-camber terrain.

Very aggressive rock crawling, long climbs at sustained high throttle (a regear to 4.10 is worthwhile if this is common), and trails rated 8 or above on the Jeep difficulty scale. Those are the cases where you start looking at the Dana 30 front axle and thinking about lockers.

title: Radiator Upgrade for the LJ 4.0L
summary: The 4.0L inline-six is a proven, thermally stable engine under normal conditions — but push it hard on a hot day with a heavy load in low range and the factory radiator's limits become apparent. A 2-row aluminum radiator adds meaningful cooling capacity and eliminates the failure point of the original plastic-tank design. If the factory radiator is 10 or more years old, this isn't an upgrade — it's maintenance.
description:
The LJ uses the same engine bay and radiator mounting as the TJ. The Mishimoto MMRAD-WRA-97 covers all 1997–2006 Wranglers, which means the same part fits every LJ regardless of trim level. There is no LJ-specific radiator variant required.

The factory radiator is an aluminum core with plastic end tanks crimped onto it. The plastic tanks harden and crack with age, and the crimped connections between plastic and aluminum leak as the materials expand and contract at different rates. An all-aluminum radiator eliminates both failure modes. A 2-row aluminum core also moves more coolant volume per pass, which directly reduces peak operating temperature under load.

If the radiator is original and the LJ has over 80,000 miles, inspect the plastic tanks carefully. Any discoloration, surface crazing, hairline cracks, or seepage at the tank-to-core seam is grounds for immediate replacement — a failed radiator on trail or on a remote overland route is a serious problem. Replace it before it fails, not after.

If the radiator is relatively new and you're chasing a genuine overheating concern, check the thermostat, water pump, and cooling fan clutch first. A weak fan clutch is the more common culprit on a high-mileage 4.0L than a failed radiator.

The Mishimoto MMRAD-WRA-97 is a direct bolt-in replacement. All factory hose locations, mounting tabs, and transmission cooler fittings are in the same position. Installation is 2–3 hours including a proper drain, flush, and refill with fresh coolant. Comes with a lifetime warranty. At $280 it's the price/value leader.

Griffin's all-aluminum unit uses slightly heavier-gauge core material and is made in the USA. At $370 it's the premium choice for a high-mileage engine that works hard. Both Griffin and Mishimoto outperform the factory plastic-tank unit in sustained high-load conditions.

title: Dual Battery and Charging System Upgrade for the LJ
summary: The 4.0L's factory alternator outputs 90 amps — adequate for a stock Wrangler but increasingly strained as you add accessories. A winch can draw 400+ amps at load, LED light bars pull 10–20 amps continuously, and a fridge or compressor adds another 5–15 amps. Running all of this off a single starting battery and a marginal alternator is the path to a dead battery in camp and a surprise winch failure mid-recovery. A dual-battery system with proper charging is the fix.
description:
The LJ's engine bay is more crowded than a TJ's since the longer body adds very little space up front. A Group 31 AGM battery will fit in the stock battery location; the secondary battery needs a purpose-built bracket or a custom mount in the engine bay on the driver's side or behind the seat.

AGM (Absorbed Glass Mat) batteries tolerate deep discharge and recharge cycles that would kill a conventional flooded lead-acid. For an auxiliary battery that runs a fridge, lights, and radio overnight and then gets recharged on the drive out, AGM is the right technology. The Northstar NSB-AGM31 is a high-quality Group 31 AGM with genuine deep-cycle capacity. The Optima Yellow Top is a smaller, more popular option that works well in the auxiliary role.

A simple diode-based battery isolator (like the Sure Power 1315A) keeps the batteries isolated until the alternator voltage rises, then charges both. It's cheap and works. The downside: the isolator allows the starting battery to be depleted by accessories if the isolation diode voltage drop is wrong, and it doesn't charge the auxiliary battery as efficiently as a DC-DC charger. A DC-DC charger like the Redarc BCDC1225D is smarter: it regulates charging voltage specifically for AGM chemistry and fully charges the secondary even when the alternator is loaded by other accessories. For a serious overland build, the DC-DC charger is worth the extra cost.

The most important rule for the 4.0L's 90-amp alternator: **always warm the engine before extended winching**. At idle, the alternator may only produce 65–70 amps — not enough to offset the winch draw. Run the engine at 1,500 RPM during sustained winching to maximize alternator output and minimize battery voltage drop. With a dual-battery setup, you have more reserve capacity if the alternator can't keep up during a single hard pull.

The primary battery feeds the starting system and winch (direct-wired with its own fuse). The secondary battery feeds accessories — lights, fridge, compressor, radio. The DC-DC charger or isolator connects between the two batteries. Run appropriate fusing on every circuit and use 2/0 AWG cable for the winch connections regardless of battery count.

title: LED Light Bar and Pod Lighting for the LJ

parts.name: Baja Designs Squadron Sport (A-pillar pods, pair)
KC HiLites Gravity LED Pro6 30" light bar
Rigid Industries Radiance Pod Scene Lights (pair)
Roof rack light bar mount bracket

summary: The LJ has a natural advantage for overhead LED lighting: its longer roof offers more mounting real estate than a TJ, and a roof rack on the LJ sits far enough from the cab that a 30-inch light bar doesn't blind the driver in reflective conditions. A-pillar pod lights handle the close-range fill. Together they transform the LJ's useful range after dark.
description:
Auxiliary LED lighting is one of the most useful trail and overland upgrades, but the wiring approach makes or breaks the system. Direct wiring to the ignition or fuse block overloads circuits not designed for continuous 15–20A lighting loads. Every auxiliary light installation should use a relay: the switch triggers the relay coil, and the relay carries the load current directly from the battery.

The LJ's flat hood can mount a light bar on a low-profile hood bracket, but hood mounts put the lights in the driver's line of sight when looking down trail and can wash out the view ahead at night with reflected glare. The better option on an LJ is a roof rack with a front light bar mount — the bar sits higher, illuminates farther down trail, and the driver doesn't look through the beam. A 30-inch bar is the right size for most setups; a 40-inch bar is possible on a wide roof rack but overkill for most trails.

A-pillar mount pods provide wide-angle fill light for close-range obstacles, camp illumination, and side lighting that a forward bar doesn't cover. Baja Designs Squadron Sport pods are the gold standard at a reasonable price — they're genuinely bright, well-built, and flood-pattern pods work better for trail fill than spot. Rigid Industries Radiance pods are a solid alternative with a scene-mode option useful in camp. Mount them on the A-pillar with a manufactured bracket; avoid improvised mounts that vibrate loose on rough terrain.

Run a 30A automotive relay between the battery and each light circuit. The switch inside the cab triggers the relay coil (low current), and the relay passes load current from the battery to the lights. Install an inline fuse on the power wire within 18 inches of the battery. Ground the lights to the body metal near the mount point, not through a long wire back to the battery. Do not run the lights directly from the ignition switch or ACC fuse — those circuits are not rated for the load and will cause problems.

A roof-mounted light bar that illuminates the road ahead while driving on a public highway is illegal in most U.S. states — the lights must be covered on public roads. Add a switch cover or a removable lens cover and only run the bar off-road.

title: Winch Electrical Install for the LJ

parts.name: Warn VR12000-S Winch (12,000 lb, synthetic rope)

citations.title: Winch wiring best practices — Warn Industries

summary: The LJ is a heavier vehicle than the TJ — stock weight runs around 3,700 lbs and loaded for overland it can push 4,200 lbs. A 12,000-lb winch is the minimum; a 12,500-lb unit gives you better pulling margin in the self-recovery case where the rated capacity is reduced by the angle. The electrical side is straightforward, but it must be done correctly — tapping into existing wiring instead of running dedicated cables will cause voltage drop, overheating, and eventually a fire.
description:
Winch wiring is not complicated, but it does require respecting the current draw. A 12,000-lb winch at full load pulls 400–500 amps. This is not a circuit you can daisy-chain off an existing fuse block. It gets its own dedicated wiring from the battery, its own fuse, and its own ground.

Use 2/0 AWG (pronounced "two aught") welding cable for the winch power and ground runs. Do not use standard automotive primary wire — it's not rated for the continuous high-current draw. Welding cable is flexible, copper-stranded, and rated for the load. Run both the positive and negative cables directly from the battery to the winch solenoid; use appropriate ring terminals and apply heat-shrink to every connection.

Install a 150A ANL fuse on the positive cable within 18 inches of the battery positive terminal. This is the critical safety requirement — a short anywhere in the run between the battery and the winch solenoid is stopped by this fuse before it can start a fire. The fuse holder mounts near the battery; some owners mount it on the firewall near the battery tray.

The Warn VR12000-S is the standard recommendation: sealed motor, synthetic rope, and a track record of reliability. The Zeon 12-S is lighter and faster, worth the premium on a rig where weight matters. The Superwinch Talon 12.5i is the value option — it's not as refined as Warn but it works and costs significantly less. On an LJ used for overland, the Warn VR or Zeon is worth paying for; the quality shows up on trip three when you actually need it.

The factory wiring on the LJ is not sized for winch loads. Do not tap the ignition, the accessory bus, or any fuse block circuit. The winch gets its own direct connection. The control cable (typically a 10-12 AWG signal wire) can connect to a switched ignition source for the wireless remote module, but the power cables go straight to the battery.

title: Cold Air Intake for the LJ 4.0L

parts.name: K&N Typhoon Cold Air Intake (97-06 Wrangler 4.0L)
AEM Brute Force Cold Air Intake

summary: A cold air intake is the easiest and cheapest performance modification on the 4.0L — remove the airbox, install the intake tube and cone filter, done in an hour. Expect a 5–8 horsepower improvement and noticeably crisper throttle response, particularly at highway speeds. The 4.0L responds well because the factory airbox is restrictive by design; a less restrictive cone filter and larger intake tube frees up the breathing.
description:
The LJ's longer hood and engine bay are identical in layout to the TJ from the firewall forward — the intake tube routes the same way and all TJ-spec cold air intake kits fit the LJ without modification. If a kit lists compatibility for 1997–2006 Wrangler TJ 4.0L, it fits the LJ.

5–8 horsepower on a 190-hp engine is a 3–4% improvement. You will feel the throttle response improvement more than you'll see it on a dyno, and the intake sound at full throttle is noticeably better — the characteristic 4.0L intake roar becomes more pronounced. This is not a transformation upgrade; it's a modest, worthwhile improvement that costs little money and takes minimal time.

The K&N Typhoon is the most popular option for the TJ/LJ 4.0L. It's a direct-fit kit — the intake tube mounts to the factory MAF sensor location, the filter sits in the fender-mount position that keeps it away from the exhaust heat. The K&N oiled cotton gauze filter flows well and can be cleaned and re-oiled rather than replaced. At $190 it's the price leader.

The Volant system uses a closed box around the filter to more fully isolate the intake air from underhood heat. In theory this delivers a small additional benefit in hot weather by ensuring the air feeding the filter is genuinely cooler than ambient underhood temperature. In practice the difference is marginal on a trail rig. At $280, the Volant is worth considering if you regularly operate in high ambient temperature conditions.

The AEM Brute Force is comparable to the K&N in performance and construction — a direct-fit tube with a dry-type filter. At $200, it's a reasonable alternative if you prefer not to deal with re-oiling a K&N filter.

A cone filter in the fender area is closer to water during a stream crossing than a factory airbox. If you do water crossings regularly, consider a snorkel or ensure the filter sits above the water level you'll encounter. The AEM filter is specifically marketed as water-resistant; the K&N should not be fully submerged.

title: Seat Upgrade for the LJ
summary: The LJ's factory seats are unchanged from the TJ — the same vinyl bench-style seats that sacrifice lateral support for ease of manufacture. They're tolerable on a 30-minute drive to the trailhead and miserable on a 6-hour overland transit. Upgrading to a proper bolstered seat is one of the best comfort investments on an LJ, and since the LJ is often the vehicle for longer hauls, it pays back quickly.
description:
The seat mounting pattern in the LJ is standard TJ, so every TJ-compatible seat upgrade applies directly. No adapter plates or modification needed for any of the seats listed here — they bolt in using the factory mounting holes.

The Corbeau LG1 is the most popular TJ/LJ seat upgrade for good reason. It has meaningful lateral bolstering, a high back for head support on highway driving, and uses a fiberglass shell with foam padding that holds up to trail use. It's not a race seat — it reclines and feels like a normal bucket rather than a track seat — which makes it livable for the daily/overland use case. At $280 per seat, a pair fits most budgets alongside a build. The LG1 comes in black vinyl or fabric and both hold up well in a soft-top environment.

The Smittybilt XRC foam seat is the budget choice. At $170/seat it's a significant step up from factory in support and bolstering. The foam is firmer than factory, the high-back provides better support on rough terrain, and the seat holds its shape through a season of use. The finish is basic and the mounting hardware is marginal — use quality hardware when installing. For a build that's spending money on drivetrain and tires, the XRC is a respectable choice that makes a real difference.

The Mastercraft Baja RS is a proper performance seat with significantly more lateral support than the Corbeau or Smittybilt. It's designed for rally and rock crawler use where you're moving aggressively and need to stay planted in the seat. The reclining mechanism means it's not as uncomfortable on long drives as a fixed-back seat, and the materials are genuinely high-quality. At $480/seat it's a commitment; justified for a dedicated rock crawler or a serious overlander who spends real time in the driver's seat.

A 4-point harness on a rock crawler is worth considering with the Corbeau or Mastercraft — both have slots for a harness shoulder belt. The Corbeau bolt-in harness ($120) works with the LG1 and provides meaningful retention on steep side-hill terrain. For trail use at moderate speeds, a 3-point OEM-style belt with a bolstered seat is sufficient for most people; the harness is for dedicated rock crawler builds.

title: Soft Top Replacement for the LJ

citations.title: Bestop Trektop NX for LJ Unlimited

summary: The LJ's longer wheelbase requires a soft top sized specifically for the Unlimited body — the top is approximately 10 inches longer than a TJ 2-door top, and the bows and frame are different. This is not a case where "TJ compatible" means it works. If the listing doesn't specifically say LJ Unlimited or LJ, it will not fit correctly and the rear corners will gap, leak, and flap.
description:
When the factory soft top starts to crack, shrink, or delaminate — typically at 8–12 years old — replacement is the fix. The LJ aftermarket for tops is smaller than the TJ's because fewer LJs were built, but the main manufacturers all offer LJ-specific versions of their popular tops.

The Bestop Trektop NX is the best soft top available for the LJ. It uses a textured Twill fabric (Bestop's proprietary weave) that's more durable than standard vinyl, doesn't shrink or crack in cold weather, and has significantly better UV resistance. The installation uses a modular bow design that makes removal and storage easier than a traditional soft top. The NX's window seals are tighter than budget tops and the zip-in rear window is heavier vinyl than cheaper alternatives. At $600 it's the premium pick but built to last significantly longer.

The Smittybilt Premium LJ top is $310 and delivers functional weather protection. The vinyl is thicker than some budget tops, the rear window is a zip-in design, and the fit on LJ-specific units is good. Build quality is below Bestop in fit-and-finish details — seams, zip quality, and edge finishing — but it does the job. For a budget build or a rig used hard on trail where the top is secondary, the Smittybilt is a reasonable choice.

Black Mountain makes direct replacements for OEM Jeep soft tops and their LJ unit is a solid mid-tier option. Fabric quality and seam construction sit between Smittybilt and Bestop. Worth considering if the Bestop is out of budget but you want better than the Smittybilt.

The LJ's bow frame is longer than the TJ's. If you're sourcing a replacement top to use with your existing bows, confirm the top's pocket dimensions are correct for LJ bows. Mixing TJ bows with an LJ top or vice versa results in a top that won't seat correctly. When in doubt, buy the complete kit with bows included.

title: Overland Setup for the LJ

citations.title: Garvin Adventure Rack for LJ Unlimited
ARB awning and fridge product pages

summary: The LJ's 103.5-inch wheelbase is not just a stability advantage on trail — it's cargo space. The extra 10 inches over a TJ translates directly to a larger area behind the rear seat, and the longer roof provides a genuine roof rack platform. A 2-person overland rig without a trailer is achievable on the LJ where it would require compromises on a TJ. The constraint is weight: keep the loaded LJ under 4,500 lbs and the 4.0L handles the load without strain.
description:
The LJ's GVWR is around 4,300 lbs. Stock, it runs around 3,700 lbs. That gives you roughly 600 lbs of payload before you're at rated GVWR — less than it sounds once you add a roof rack, roof tent, gear, water, and two people. Plan the weight budget explicitly, not as an afterthought.

The Garvin Adventure Rack is the recommended LJ-specific rack. It mounts to the factory hard points on the LJ's body and is sized for the longer Unlimited wheelbase. Smittybilt and Tuffy also make LJ-compatible racks. The rack provides the platform for a forward light bar, an awning mount, and optionally a roof tent. A full roof rack with gear adds 80–150 lbs to the top of the vehicle; keep this in mind for center-of-gravity calculations on side-hill terrain.

The area behind the rear seat in an LJ is significantly larger than in a TJ. A rear cargo platform over the spare tire carrier provides additional protected storage. Tuffy makes a security console for the LJ interior. The rear cargo space typically fits: a 47L fridge/freezer, a bag with sleeping gear, and a 5-gallon water container without requiring a cargo trailer.

The overland LJ needs a dual battery setup. Running a 47L compressor fridge overnight draws approximately 3–5 Ah per hour depending on ambient temperature. An 80 Ah auxiliary AGM battery provides 2–3 nights of fridge operation without recharging. Add a DC-DC charger to keep the auxiliary topped off on the drive. See the dual-battery-lj entry for the full electrical setup.

An ARB 2500mm awning mounts to the roof rack side rail and deploys in under 2 minutes. For a 2-person camp, a 2500mm awning covers the cooking and kitchen area completely. Mount it on the driver's side so the camp kitchen setup is sheltered. The ARB awning includes the main canopy; the side walls are sold separately and add full enclosure for wet weather.

A realistic loaded LJ overland weight budget:
- Stock vehicle: ~3,700 lbs
- Roof rack + tent: +120 lbs
- Rear bumper + spare: +80 lbs
- Rock sliders: +60 lbs
- Fridge + contents: +75 lbs
- Water (5 gal): +42 lbs
- Gear (camping, tools, clothing): +150 lbs
- Two occupants: +340 lbs

That totals around 4,567 lbs — over the GVWR. Trim the gear to stay under 4,500 lbs and consider a suspension upgrade to handle the load correctly. A heavier spring rate in the rear is common on loaded LJ overlanders.

title: Recovery Gear Starter Kit for the LJ

parts.name: Smittybilt X2O 12K Winch (if not yet installed)

summary: Recovery gear is the equipment you need before you need the winch — and sometimes instead of it. The LJ's extra weight over the TJ (roughly 200 lbs stock, more when loaded) means the rated strap and shackles need to match the vehicle, not just the Wrangler category broadly. Size everything to the LJ's actual weight.
description:
A proper recovery kit for an LJ has five items: a rated snatch strap, two rated D-ring shackles, a traction board set, a tree saver strap, and ideally a winch. The winch is covered separately. Everything else assembles into a kit you carry on every trip.

An ARB 30-foot snatch strap rated at 17,600 lbs covers an LJ with margin. The "snatch" in snatch strap refers to the elasticity that allows a kinetic recovery — the vehicle pulls, the strap stretches and stores energy, then releases it to jerk the stuck vehicle free without requiring a constant tow. A tow strap is not a recovery strap: it has no elasticity and transfers shock load directly to both vehicles. Use a snatch strap for kinetic recovery and keep the tow strap for flat-ground towing only.

Use rated bow shackles — 3/4-inch minimum, with a working load limit marked on the shackle. Bubba Rope, ARB, and Factor 55 all make quality shackles in the $20–30/each range. Screw the pin closed and back it off a quarter turn so it can't self-tighten under load and become impossible to remove. Do not use hardware store chain links, carabiners, or anything without a stamped WLL rating.

This is a safety-critical rule. A trailer ball under recovery load can shear off and become a high-velocity projectile. Factory bumper loops are similarly not rated for kinetic recovery forces. The only correct attachment points are rated D-ring mounts on a steel bumper, or a dedicated receiver-mounted recovery point. If your LJ doesn't have a steel bumper yet, the recovery gear is still worth owning — attach to the frame using a proper tree saver looped around the frame rail, not a ball hitch.

MAXTRAX MKII traction boards are the standard — they're rated for up to 5,500 lbs per board, work in sand, mud, and snow, and pack flat under the cargo floor or on the roof rack. On an LJ with overland gear aboard, traction boards are often faster than rigging a winch for a simple stuck-in-mud situation. Carry two.

title: Winch Selection and Mount for the LJ

citations.title: Synthetic vs steel winch cable comparison — Warn

summary: The LJ is the Wrangler that goes farther and stays longer, which makes a winch more important on this platform than on a weekend-warrior TJ. A 12,000-lb synthetic rope winch is the right specification: it handles the LJ's loaded weight, is safer when a line parts, and floats — a line in the water at a creek crossing won't sink on you. Plan for the bumper first, then the winch.
description:
The first rule of winch selection for an LJ: you need a winch-compatible steel front bumper before the winch goes on. A winch bolted to a factory plastic bumper is not a recovery setup — it's a liability. Confirm the bumper's winch plate is rated for the winch you're installing before you buy either one.

Synthetic rope is the correct choice for a trail and overland winch in 2024. When steel cable breaks under load it stores enormous energy and whips with lethal force. Synthetic rope breaks with far less stored energy, is lighter, and is far safer to handle and re-spool. It's also rated for the same loads as equivalent-diameter steel. The one downside is that synthetic rope degrades from UV exposure and abrasion more quickly — inspect it before every trip and retire it when you see fraying.

The general rule is to select a winch rated for 1.5x the vehicle's gross weight. The LJ's GVWR is around 4,300 lbs loaded. A 9,500-lb winch is undersized for a self-recovery situation on a loaded LJ, particularly on an incline. At 12,000 lbs you have genuine margin for the difficult case: pulling yourself out of a deep hole at an angle.

The VR12000-S is Warn's mid-range sealed winch with synthetic rope. The sealed housing handles water crossings; the Series motor is reliable and field-repairable. This is the standard recommendation for an LJ that does moderate to hard trail and overland. It's not the fastest winch in the lineup but it's proven.

The Zeon 12 is lighter, faster, and costs significantly more. The planetary gear design spools faster than a worm-gear winch, which matters when you're recovering on a hard technical trail and need to move quickly. If the LJ is a dedicated trail rig and weight and speed matter, the Zeon is worth the premium. For most overlanders, the VR12000-S is sufficient.

The Superwinch Talon 12.5i is the value option — 12,500 lbs, synthetic rope, and a lower price point than either Warn. It's not as refined in fit, finish, or waterproofing as the Warn products, but it functions correctly and is a meaningful upgrade over cheap harbor-freight-style winches. On a budget build, the Talon works.

title: Death Wobble Diagnosis

citations.title: LJ Wrangler specs — CJ Pony Parts

summary: The LJ shares the TJ's coil-sprung, track-bar-located front axle, so it gets the same death wobble when a front-end joint wears. The violent shake after a bump at speed is the symptom; a worn track bar, tie-rod end, or ball joint is the cause. Find the worn part before you drive it again.
description:
Death wobble is a safety issue — if it has started, take the LJ off the highway until it is fixed. The loop is the same on every coil Wrangler: a worn locating joint lets the front axle oscillate, the oscillation feeds through the steering, and only braking to a crawl settles it.

The most common trigger is the track bar — both its ends and the frame-side mount, which elongates over time and on lifted trucks. Grab the bar and try to move it at each end and at the bracket; any play means replace it. The LJ's longer wheelbase does not change this — the front-end geometry is pure TJ.

With the front lifted and supported on the frame, check tie-rod ends and the drag link for play, ball joints at 12-and-6, and control-arm bushings for cracks. Re-torque the track bar and control-arm bolts to factory spec — a loose factory bolt mimics a worn part. Out-of-balance tires and loose wheel bearings can trigger or amplify wobble, so include them.

A bigger steering stabilizer hides the onset and lets the worn joint keep degrading until something lets go at speed. Replace what is worn, torque to spec, and the LJ tracks straight — the stabilizer is then a refinement, not a crutch. One LJ-specific note: the longer wheelbase can make a mild shimmy feel less violent than on a TJ, which tempts owners to ignore it. Do not. The same worn joint that produces a survivable wobble at 45 mph produces a dangerous one at 70, and the fix is the same inexpensive part either way.

title: Lift Kit Guide: The Long-Wheelbase Advantage

citations.title: LJ Wrangler specs — CJ Pony Parts

summary: The LJ lifts exactly like a TJ — coil springs and longer shocks — but its 103.5-inch wheelbase changes the math in your favor. The extra 10 inches between the axles makes the LJ more stable on a lifted suspension and far less tippy than a short TJ, so a 3–4 inch coil kit on 33s is a genuinely capable, well-mannered build.
description:
Verdict: a quality 3–4" coil kit with an adjustable front track bar is the right LJ build for 33s, and it behaves better on-road and on off-camber than the same lift on a TJ. The long wheelbase spreads the weight and calms the ride; the tradeoff is a slightly lower breakover angle, so belly and gas-tank skid protection matter a touch more.

Raising a coil, track-bar-located front axle without re-centering it is what triggers death wobble. An adjustable front track bar is mandatory above 3 inches. Add adjustable or correction-bracket control arms to put caster back in range, extended brake lines for the added droop, and front sway-bar disconnects so the front axle can flex — the TJ/LJ short arms otherwise bind.

Above ~3.5 inches the rear driveline angle needs attention: a slip-yoke eliminator with a CV driveshaft is the proper cure, not a transfer-case drop. For tires, 33s are the sweet spot on a 3–4" lift; 35s want more lift, a regear (4.88+), and a front-axle plan since the non-Rubicon front is a Dana 30.

Same lift parts as a TJ, better road manners. Build it to 33s, correct the geometry, and the LJ is the Wrangler that does long highway stretches and hard trails without compromise.

title: Tire Fitment Guide for the LJ

citations.title: LJ Wrangler specifications — CJ Pony Parts

summary: The LJ's longer wheelbase — 103.5 inches versus the TJ's 93.5 — changes the tire equation in a meaningful way. The wider track between axles improves stability at larger tire sizes, reduces the tipping tendency under loaded trail conditions, and makes the LJ more comfortable on corrugated dirt roads with bigger tires than a TJ would be. The LJ genuinely gets more out of 33s on 3.5 inches of lift than a shorter Wrangler does.
description:
Tire sizing on the LJ follows the same rules as any solid-axle coil-sprung Wrangler: more lift enables larger tires, larger tires require a regear to maintain usable performance, and fender and body clearance is what physically limits how wide you can go. Know the constraints at each level before spending money.

The factory LJ sits on 30-inch tires. With zero lift and stock wheels, 30s clear without rubbing. Some owners squeeze 31s with careful wheel positioning, but rubbing on full turn lock is common. At stock height, stay at 30s or accept trimming.

A 2-inch body or coil lift gets you to 31-inch tires with minor trimming of the inner fender liners at full lock. Shackle or spring spacer lifts at 2 inches are common in this tier. Wheel backspacing matters: 3.75-inch backspacing on a 15x8 wheel gives clearance without spacers.

A 3–4 inch coil lift with 33x12.5R15 tires is the correct LJ build for most people. It fits without major fender surgery, the LJ's long wheelbase keeps it stable, and 33s on a 4.0L with the right gearing (4.10 or 4.56 depending on transmission) is genuinely capable. Trim the inner fender liner but leave the outer flares intact. Get an adjustable front track bar above 3 inches. Regear to 4.10 at minimum; 4.56 is better.

At 35s the requirements stack up: 4.5 inches or more of lift, a regear to 4.88 or 5.13, fender trimming or flat replacement flares, and a front-axle plan since the non-Rubicon Dana 30 is marginal at 35s (the Rubicon's Dana 44 front is fine). The LJ's long wheelbase helps stability but the breakover angle gets worse as the suspension lifts higher. Belly skid protection becomes more critical.

33-inch tires on the LJ with a 4.0L and AX-15 manual work acceptably on factory 3.73 gears, but it's soft. Regearing to 4.10 is the minimum improvement. With 35s, 4.88 is the target for the automatic (42RLE) and 5.13 is the target for the manual, which then pairs well with the AX-15's final gear ratios and the NP231's low range.

title: Wheel Selection for the LJ

citations.title: Pro Comp steel wheel fitment guide

summary: The LJ uses the same 5x4.5-inch bolt pattern (5x114.3mm) as every TJ and JK Wrangler — a wheel that fits a TJ fits an LJ. The meaningful variables are diameter, width, and backspacing. Get the backspacing wrong and you'll rub the inner fender liner at full articulation, or the tire will protrude past the flare and you'll have a legal and aesthetic problem. Get it right and the wheel disappears as a variable.
description:
Wheel selection for the LJ comes down to budget and intended use: steel 15-inch wheels are cheap, strong, and the right choice for trail use where a rock strike might damage a wheel; 17-inch alloy wheels are lighter, look better, and allow better brake clearance and tire selection but cost significantly more and can be damaged by the same trail use.

A 15x8-inch steel wheel with 3.75-inch backspacing is the correct fitment for 33x12.5R15 tires on a 3–4-inch lift. Pro Comp and Mickey Thompson both make well-priced steel wheels in this size. At $75–95 each, a set of five (including the spare) runs $375–475 — the budget-friendly option. Steel bends where alloy cracks; a bent steel wheel can often be hammered back into use on trail where a cracked alloy wheel cannot.

Method 305 NV and Fuel Assault are two well-regarded 17x9-inch alloy options at moderate prices. The 17-inch diameter opens up a wider selection of 33 and 35-inch tires with lower sidewall aspect ratios. Method's 305 is designed specifically for off-road use with a bead ring that improves bead retention at low pressure. At $185–220 each the cost is real — a set of five will run $925–1,100.

For 33x12.5R15 on a stock to 4-inch lift: 3.75-inch backspacing clears the brake caliper and positions the tire so it doesn't rub the inner fender at full droop. With a 4.5-inch lift and 35s, you may need a 4.5-inch backspacing to keep the tire from rubbing the front fender at full lock — measure before committing. Running a spacer to push a wheel outboard is acceptable for small adjustments but adds a wear surface; get the backspacing right on the wheel purchase.

Every LJ uses 5x4.5" (5x114.3mm), 1/2-20 lug nuts, 71.5mm center bore. Confirm center bore or use hub rings — a wheel with a 73.1mm center bore will fit on a hub ring but will vibrate without one.
